 1.1 Construction Stage Manager (CSG)
 Executed in mode CSG, TALPA supports the automatic generation of a analysis sequence, based on an intuitive description of the single construction stages. The actual calculation is then executed in mode FEA.
 Description of the construction stages is based on element groups and the philosophy that only changes in relation to the previous construction stage (e.g. installation, removal, change of properties of element groups) are specified. Groups that remain unchanged (and therefore are based on the foregoing construction stage), are treated automatically.
 In CSG-mode input records CSYS, CCRL, CS, CGRP, CLOA, CGW and ECHO are evaluated.
 Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
 In FEA mode TALPA allows for linear or non-linear analysis of stresses and deformations both for
 arbitrary shaped plane structures that are loaded in-plane (plane stress or plane strain conditions)
 •
 and axisymmetric three-dimensional structures
 by means of the finite element method. The main focus of TALPA is the numerical analysis of geotechnical related taks and soil mechanics.
 The analysis requires a descretized system (splitting of the structure into an assembly of indi- vidual elements interconnected at nodes) that is stored in the data base. TALPA features the following element types:
 planar continuum elements
 • beam elements
 spring/ interface elements
 cable elements
 truss elements
 All element types offer various optional nonlinear effects, allowing for an effective and realistic capturing of relevant mechanical effects regarding the structure’s load carrying characteris- tics. This involves in particular interaction between soil and structural members including wall- friction and nonlinear load carrying characteristics of soil. Other important aspects, to name a
 few, are load transfer via (grouted) anchors, load redistribution capabilities of geo-grids, yield- ing/ tensile failure of struts, formation of plastic hinges and nonlinear load carrying behavior of (reinforced) concrete members.
 The program handles structures with rigid or elastic types of support. Elastic support can be provided linearly distributed or point-wise. Additionally, rigid elements or skew supports can be taken into account.

At the left side of the figure, there is a **vertical axis labeled “y”** near the bottom. A solid downward arrowhead marks the positive direction of the **y-axis**. The horizontal reference line extends across the top portion of the diagram and is drawn as a straight line (serving as the **x-axis reference**). There is no explicit “x” label visible, but the horizontal line functions as the x-axis in the plane.

Near the upper-left quadrant, just below where the vertical and horizontal lines meet, a **curved dashed arc** indicates an **angular coordinate** labeled **“φz”**. The arc is drawn between the horizontal reference (x-direction) and the vertical axis direction, with the label positioned adjacent to the arc. This indicates the **angle around the z-axis** (hence the subscript “z”), even though the actual graphic depicts a rotation within the x–y plane.

A small pivot-like connection point is implied at the intersection of the reference lines, and the arc suggests the direction of the positive rotation. The arc is dashed and open, visually emphasizing it as a rotational parameter rather than a physical boundary.

Overall, the diagram communicates that the coordinate system is **right-handed** and uses a **plane spanned by the X- and Y-axes**. The parameter **φz** represents the planar rotation about the **z-axis**, consistent with the provided context: positive rotation is defined by a **clockwise rotation of X about the Z-axis** when viewing corresponds to the positive z-direction. The diagram therefore functions as a compact schematic for **in-plane orientation** using a single angular degree of freedom.

Plane systems are located in the plane spanned by the X- and Y-axes of a cartesian coordinate system. This system is right-handed; a positive rotation is therefore defined by a clockwise rotation of X about the Z-axis (view corresponds to positive Z-direction). Plane systems are
 loaded in-plane, exclusively.

TALPA supports three basic analysis models:
 The total strain normal to the structure’s plane is zero. The thickness of the planar elements defaults to 1.0 m. Orientation of the coordinate system can be chosen arbitrarily; however, it is common practice to have the global Y-direction aligned with the gravity direction.
 This model allows for the analysis of axisymmetric structures under axisymmetric loads. In this case, the mesh represents a meridional section, rotating about the X axis. The analysis is based on a circular element spanning an angle of 1 rad. Essential characteristics of the axisymmetric analysis model are:
 – The appearance of a circular strain.
 – Supports in Y-direction are not a necessary condition for a kinematically stable system.
 – The dimension of nodal loads is no longer kN, instead kN/m circumference is used. Line loads change from kN/m to kN/m2 and bedding constants from kN/m2 to kN/m3.
 – Beam elements cannot be used together with axisymmetric elements.
 The stresses perpendicular to the structure’s plane are zero (e.g. building walls). Orienta- tion of the coordinate system can be chosen arbitrarily; however, it is common practice to have the global Y-direction aligned with the gravity direction. Friction materials (soil materi- als) are not a valid option for this model.

Truss and cable elements can only transmit axial forces. In order to restrict the cable reaction to tensile force transfer, a nonlinear analysis is required.
 Optional nonlinear effects are:
 • Initial slip (GAP)
 • Tensile failure upon reaching tensile rupture force (CRAC)
 • Yielding (YIEL)
 • Reaction according to a specified material work law (AQUA: SSLA).
 Hint
 When simulating a loading history using primary states, the following should be consid- ered:
 GAP is related to the total deformation of the element.
 CRAC Straining beyond the element’s tensile strength yields to an immediate drop of the tensile capacity to zero. This damage cannot be recovered, tensile forces are no longer transfered by the element – even after a complete load reversal. Continuing loading yields crack growth. Compression cannot be transfered unless the crack has closed completely, i.e. the total deformation must become negative.

The image is a schematic figure labeled **“Figure 2.2: Standard nonlinear spring response curves.”** It contains **three small, side-by-side graphs** illustrating how the **axial spring force** \(P\) responds to **displacement** \(V\) for different nonlinear behaviors. The axes in each sub-graph include:

- A **vertical axis** labeled **\(P\)** (force), with an arrow indicating positive upward direction.
- A **horizontal axis** labeled **\(V\)** (displacement), with an arrow indicating positive rightward direction in the first two panels.
- Dashed vertical and horizontal markings indicate transition points and reference levels.

### Left panel (GAP / slip behavior)
The leftmost panel shows a **piecewise linear force–displacement curve**. Near the origin, there is a **horizontal “dead zone”** (force remains zero while displacement occurs), labeled **“GAP.”** The label appears on both sides of the center line (upper-left and lower-left), implying a symmetric slack/slip region for positive and negative displacement. Once the GAP is exceeded, the curve turns into a **stiffening linear segment** that rises with displacement: a slanted line indicates the spring engages after slack is taken up. The “GAP” is shown with a bracket-like annotation and arrows pointing to the slack interval.

### Middle panel (CRAC / tensile failure)
The middle panel displays a force response that is **linear on one side** but shows **rupture behavior on the other**. The curve rises along a slanted line for one displacement direction, while on the opposite side the force **drops to a reduced or constant level** and is annotated **“CRAC”** (tensile rupture). A vertical dashed marker and a label “RISS” (crack) appear near the transition, indicating that when tensile force reaches a rupture threshold, the spring loses tensile capacity. The graph resembles a bilinear/step-like response: intact in compression/tension (depending on sign convention) but failing in tension beyond the critical point.

### Right panel (+-FILE / failure behavior in rupture/compression)
The rightmost panel includes a small schematic of a **force–displacement curve that includes a sudden change in slope or truncation**, with a label that includes **“+/- FILE.”** There are dashed reference lines marking the transition level, and the curve shows that beyond the threshold, the force does not continue increasing normally. This panel suggests a **failure or yielding-type limit** (consistent with standard nonlinear spring options mentioned in the context: tensile rupture, yielding, and failure).

### Overall interpretation
Across the figure, the spring is depicted as having **standard nonlinear response modes** such as:
- **Initial slip (GAP)** (left panel),
- **Tensile cracking/rupture (CRAC)** (middle panel),
- **A further failure/limit response** (right panel).

The annotations and piecewise linear shapes emphasize that the nonlinear effects alter the spring’s effective stiffness and/or force capacity depending on whether displacement drives the system into the relevant regime (slack taken up, tensile rupture reached, etc.).

The image is a small schematic diagram illustrating a 2D rigid frictional interface element in its unloaded state (labeled “Figure 2.3: 2D interface element in its unloaded state”). The drawing shows a horizontal interface segment between two circular node symbols at the left and right ends. The left node is labeled “1’ ” (a primed node identifier), and the right node is labeled “2”. Two short red dashed markers (or small red segments) appear along the interface area, suggesting the element location/extent along the structural line.

A thick black horizontal line represents the interface element geometry in the unloaded configuration. On the right end, there is a small “2” near the circular node, and a vertical dimension annotation “1.0” is shown to the right, indicating the total length or scale reference for the schematic (likely the height/size reference in the figure layout). Near the center-top of the diagram, there is a vertical red arrow labeled “X” pointing upward. Next to the arrow is a horizontal red dashed label “Y” or “γ” (the text appears as “Y” with a small Greek-like symbol shape), indicating the local coordinate axes used to define interface actions.

The coordinate system is depicted with the upward red arrow corresponding to the local x-axis, described in the accompanying context as perpendicular to the interface edge, pointing from the interface edge toward the opposite edge. A second local direction (local y-axis) is indicated by the “Y” label on the horizontal axis at the top of the figure (drawn as a curved/angled reference typical in schematic coordinate depictions). The overall styling is minimal and intended for topological and kinematic clarity: the key message is that the interface element is a zero-thickness (or very small thickness-to-length ratio) 2D element connecting two nodal points, with a defined local coordinate system governing axial (normal) and shear (tangential) responses.

No material bodies (soil/structure) are drawn—only the element itself and its coordinate axes—reinforcing that this figure is primarily about geometry, node arrangement (four-node topological description is referenced in the context, though only two end nodes are visually emphasized here), and the sign convention for local axes used in rigid frictional contact models.

The image is a schematic, black-line diagram on a white background illustrating the local deformation modes of a 2D rigid frictional interface element. Two separate sub-panels are shown, each labeled with axes and small arrow indicators to clarify the sign convention.

**Left sub-panel (axial direction):**  
- A horizontal interface line is represented by a thin black bar with two labeled nodes on its ends (node **1** on the left and node **2** on the right).  
- A green horizontal segment lies along the bar, indicating the position of the interface.  
- Above the bar, two red upward arrows are drawn, both labeled **X**. The arrows point in the positive local **x-axis** direction (with the label positioned near the first arrow and another near the right), indicating deformation related to the **axial action** of the interface.  
- Near the interior of the bar, a pair of small red markers or dots indicate the interface discretization or reference points.  
- On the right side of this left panel, a vertical black dimension line is drawn with label **Δu**, indicating the axial displacement magnitude (relative movement in the direction of the local x-axis).

**Right sub-panel (shear direction):**  
- Another horizontal interface segment is shown, again with nodes labeled **1** (left) and **2** (right), but in this panel the node symbols are open circles and the connecting line is thicker black.  
- A green horizontal segment marks the interface edge region.  
- A vertical coordinate arrow labeled **X** appears at the top-right, showing the local **x-axis** is perpendicular to the interface edge.  
- A horizontal coordinate arrow labeled **Y** appears below the interface, showing the local **y-axis** is parallel to the interface edge.  
- Two red diagonal or short arrows indicate deformation in the local shear sense (one arrow pointing downward-left and one pointing upward-right), and a green dashed/curved indicator shows relative sliding direction.  
- The top right includes a red arrow pointing toward the left beneath the **X** arrow, reinforcing the shear relative motion along the interface.

Overall, the figure communicates that **rigid frictional interface elements** in 2D exhibit **two primary mechanical responses**: (1) an **axial (normal) displacement** associated with the local **x-axis** (perpendicular to the interface), measured as **Δu**, and (2) a **shear deformation** associated with the local **y-axis** (tangential to the interface), represented by the opposing arrow directions. The clean two-panel layout emphasizes sign conventions and the separation between normal and tangential deformation modes for contact/interaction modeling (e.g., soil–structure interaction or layer/slip-surface interfaces).

Rigid Frictional Interface elements can be used to simulate the contact conditions between two mechanically interacting bodies of a model. Common use cases in geotechnics include soil- structure interaction, modeling of the interface between distinct soil layers, the slip surface of an unstable slope etc.
 2D interface elements topologically consist of four nodes and are characterized by a very small thickness to length ratio, being ideally zero-thickness elements in the unloaded configuration. Therefore, two edges are formed, with the edge defined between the first two nodes being the interface edge, which lies on the side where the interface is defined. The local coordinate system is defined with local x-axis perpendicular to the interface edge and pointing towards the opposite edge (Fig. 2.3). 2D Rigid Frictional Interfaces can be generated along a structural line with the use of record SOFIMSHC: SLNS and option TYPE INTF.
 Rigid Frictional Interface elements are characterized by two distinct actions: an axial one, along local x-axis, and a shear one, along local y-axis (Fig. 2.4). Their material properties can be defined with the use of record AQUA: BMAT. The initial stiffness of interface elements is ex- pected to be very high, compared to the surrounding elements, in order to ensure an initial rigid connectivity between the two regions. Instead of explicitly defining stiffness constants, the elements may derive their stiffness by the Young’s and Shear Moduli of the material associ- ated with the bedding properties. This is possible by defining a reference thickness H, which corresponds to the finite thickness of the physical matter that the interface elements represent, despite their zero (or other) thickness on the generated mesh. An additional reduction of the shear strength may be applied, with the use of the corresponding factor RFAC.
 Hint
 If parameter H is not provided, then an appropriate finite material thickness is calculated internally, which will provide quasi-rigid but numerically robust interface elements. The automatic determination of interface material thickness is recommended.

The SOFiSTiK default ansatz for a 2D continuum element is based on the concept of enhanced assumed strains (EAS). The essential characteristics of this ansatz are shortly motivated and described in the following.
 Geometry of the plain element is topologically described by 4 nodes in the element corner points (QUAD). The standard ansatz space of a corresponding isoparametric element formu- lation using bilinear ansatz functions provides for relatively limited kinematics of the element, only. As an important consequence, a tendency towards ’locking’ can be observed for elements of this type. The well-known example of a QUAD element subjected to centric planar uniaxial bending illustrates this behavior. The element’s bilinear function space for the displacements is not able to reproduce the bending kinematics accurately - resulting in parasitic (unphysical) shear strains that induce a significant artifical stiffening of the element’s response. This effect is commonly known as (shear) ’locking’.
 To alleviate this problem, normally a strong refinement of the element discretization is required. Alternative, more efficient, options to overcome the phenomenon are
 a) a sufficient increase of the order of the element ansatz space (=more degrees of freedom per element), e.g., using ansatz functions for the displacements of quadratic, cubic and higher order;
 •
 b) an element technological, internal enhancement of the element kinematics.
 Methods falling in class b), have received great attention also adressing the issue of efficient shell element formulations. This triggered the development of numerous strategies for element enhancement.
 The basic idea of the EAS concept is based on the notion that parasitic strains are responsible for the observed locking effects. As a consequence, the EAS directly aims at enhancing the
 ansatz space for the strains by terms that are not directly induced by the ansatz for the dis- placements (assumed). This is done in such a way that the parasitic strains, possibly induced by the insufficient ansatz space for the displacements, are compensated (eliminated) by the assumed strains...

This is done in such a way that the parasitic strains, possibly induced by the insufficient ansatz space for the displacements, are compensated (eliminated) by the assumed strains....
 It can be shown that it is permissible to derive an element local formulation of the assumed strains - provided that certain constraints are considered (Simo and Hughes [1] and Simo and Rifai [2]). The essential benefit is: Elimination of the additional degrees of freedom corrspond- ing to the enhanced terms already on element level, i.e., they do not add to the global number of system unknowns (→ efficiency)!
 Further benefits:
 • Choice of element ansatz not required until computation; no remeshing required in case of changes.
 • MPC’s (multi point constraints) that allow, e.g., for consistent connection between quadratic and linear elements, are not required.
 • In contrast to many other approaches for element enhancement, adoption of the EAS con- cept in a nonlinear framework is rather straight forward and can be achieved with minor overhead, only.
 The well established Wilson/Taylor element with so called "incompatible modes" is a special case of the more general EAS concept (Simo and Rifai [2]).
 Optionally, the EAS ansatz can be suppressed via CTRL option QART 0. In this case, element behavior is controlled by isoparametric bilinear ansatz functions.
 The non-conforming types are suppressed in the case of triangular elements. For general load- ing states these elements are of very limited use since they show a strong tendency towards shear-locking - resulting in a far too stiff prediction of the system response. The adoption of this element for the analysis of general type problems is discouraged.
 For additional reading regarding this topic see, e.g., Bischoff [3] or Klinkel and Wagner [4].
 Various state-of-the-art nonlinear continuum material laws are available. For details, please refer to the AQUA manual AQUA: NMAT.

The image is a schematic diagram illustrating **nodal force balance** for a finite element in the context of the “primary states” concept.

At the center is a **gray rectangular element** (representing a finite element or element domain). Inside the element, there is a **small red vertical arrow** pointing both upward and downward in the sense of a force pair: it indicates an **internal nodal force** contribution. This internal force is shown along the element’s vertical direction, emphasizing the compressive stress state being converted into equivalent nodal (expansive) forces through element-domain integration.

Around the gray rectangle, at each side and near the corners, there are **four blue arrows** (one at each side: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right). The blue arrows are directed **toward the element from the top** and **away from the element to the bottom** (as drawn), indicating **external nodal loads** applied at the element boundaries. In the top boundary the blue arrows point downward; on the bottom boundary they point upward. Similarly, on the left and right boundaries, blue arrows point outward/inward consistently with the schematic’s nodal load pattern. This color-coding distinguishes **external loads (blue)** from **internal nodal forces (green/red)** as described in the accompanying text.

Additionally, on the left and right sides of the rectangle there are **green arrows** aligned vertically, pointing in opposite directions on the two sides (green arrows appear on both the left and right edges). These green arrows represent the **internal nodal forces** (or “expansive forces”) derived from the stress state of the primary element. Their placement on the boundaries indicates that internal forces are transferred to nodes of the element.

A key visual outcome is that the diagram depicts a situation where **the blue external nodal forces counteract the internal nodal forces at the nodes**, achieving **equilibrium**—corresponding to scenario (a) in the provided context: if external loads match those associated with the referenced primary state, the resulting force is zero and no additional deformation/stress change occurs.

The element is in a state of equilibrium, no further deformation/ change of stress evolves.

 c) No external loading in the current computation step is applied, e.g., due to deactivation of adjacent elements and consequential loss of nodal reset forces. Soil is a porous material consisting of solid particles which together represent the grain skele- ton. The pores can be filled with fluid (commonly water) and air. Hence we talk about soil as a three phase system (Figure 2.10).
 For quasi-saturated soils, an explicit consideration of the air volume V (Figure 2.10b) can be neglected and a corresponding 2-phase approach can be established. The 2-phase model explicitly accounts for (excess) pore water pressure p and effective stress σ′ acting on the grain skeleton. It relies on Terzagi’s principle of effective stresses
 σ = σ′ + p ,
 (2.15)
 where σ denotes the total stress. Combining this with the assumption of undrained conditions, i.e. flow of pore water is prevented, a relation between volumetric change and change of pore water pressure can be derived. Together, this facilitates a differentiated simulation of the evolution of pore water pressure and effective stress. Details of the model are given in (AQUA: NMAT, TYPE UNDR).
 The 2-phase model is activated by assigning undrained or drained conditions via the group control GRP TYPE UNDR/ DRAI.
 When undrained material parameters are defined and the undrained analysis is activated (cf. GRP TYPE) the stiffness of the pore water is automatically added to the stiffness of the soil skeleton.
 Distinction is then made between the effective stresses Δσ′ and pore pressures Δσ, which are saved separately in the data base.
 The second part of the Terzaghi’s principle states that all quantifiable effects of the changes in soil stresses (e.g. volume changes, shape changes, shear resistance) are a direct conse- quence of a change in effective stresses σ′. As a repercussion of this statement, the non-linear soil analysis according to the method described in this subsection is based solely on the ef- fective stresses σ′ and the effective strength (e.g. φ′, c’) and stiffness parameters (e.g. E′ , ν′).

 Soft, normally consolidated or lightly overconsolidated clays have the tendency to reduce their volume (contraction) when subjected to shear (deviatoric) stress in drained conditions. As a consequence NC soil under undrained conditions experience increase in the pore water pressure under shear. The pore pressure Δp monotonically increases with the increase of the axial deformation ε and the increase of the deviatoric stress q (Figures 2.11a and 2.12a). The effective stress path in p − q diagram (Fig. 2.12) shows that the mean effective stress p′ is reduced during the loading stage and the undrained strength is smaller than the drained strength.
 Overconsolidated clays after some small initial range of compression tend to expand (dilate) in volume under shear stress in drained conditions. As a result OC clays can experience decrease in the pore water pressure under undrained loading conditions, sometimes followed by the

 complete reversal of the sign and negative excess pore water pressure at large strains, thus having larger undrained than the drained strength (Figures 2.11b and 2.12b).
 Hint
 Undrained strength of normally consolidated soft clay can be smaller than the drained strength due to the contractive nature of NC clays. On the other hand, the undrained strength of overconsolidated clay can be larger than the drained strength due to the ten- dency of OC clays to expand when subjected to drained shear.
 Special care must be taken when selecting appropriate model of the soil. For example, Mohr- Coulomb model can significantly overestimate the undrained shear strength c, especial for the normally consolidated (NC) soil. This is illustrated in the Figure 2.13 where the effective stress path in the CU triaxial test are compared to the theoretical path obtained by the MC model.

This is illustrated in the Figure 2.13 where the effective stress path in the CU triaxial test are compared to the theoretical path obtained by the MC model.. Hint. In the undrained effective stress analysis using effective parameters the undrained shear strength c is a consequence of the model, not an input parameter..
 In the case of the MC model the material behaves linear elastic until the MC yield criterion is
 reached. According to the theory of linear elasticity the change of the effective mean stress Δp′ is linearly proportional to the change of the volumetric strain Δε, i.e. Δp′ = K′Δε. For the undrained conditions of soil saturated with water, the change of the volumetric strain Δε is very small due to the fact that the water is almost incompressible, i.e. Δε ≈ 0. This in turn means that the change of the effective mean stress Δp′ will be approx. zero - the stress paths for MC model of the triaxial CU test in p − q diagram rise vertically (see Fig. 2.13, blue line)1.
 In the MC model there will be no development of the excess pore pressure due to shear stress. As aforementioned (see Figures 2.11 and 2.12) this does not correspond to the reality because most real soils will experience change of the pore water pressure when subjected to shearing. This means that the Mohr-Coulomb model in the analysis based on the effective stress and strength parameters can overestimate the undrained shear strength (c,MC > c,re) of NC soil with contractive tendency under shearing (Figure 2.13). Neglecting this fact can have serious consequences on the structures founded on such soil, followed by the catastrophic outcome (Nicoll Highway collapse, COI et al. [5]).
 More advance models can provide better estimate for the undrained strength than the Mohr - Coulomb model. In particular the Hardening Soil model is able to model the change of the pore water pressure occurring under undrained shear loading conditions, providing a more realistic effective stress paths and values for undrained shear strength c than the MC model (Figure 2.14). However, the results of the analysis with the Hardening Soil model are very sensitive to the used model parameters and the choice of the dilatancy model2.

TALPA accounts for the elements’ various physical nonlinearities that have been outlined above when the nonlinear analysis mode is activated (SYST PROB NONL).
 Solution of the nonlinear system is done iteratively. To this end, starting from the initial state of the system (primary load case) the system displacements are varied until the correspond- ing system reactions, together with the specified external loading, form a balanced state of equilibrium (= convergence wihtin a predefined tolerance). The iterative change of the system deformation state is essentially based on a successive solution of modified linear problems. For this purpose, several procedures are available. They are described in subsequent sections.
 If a numerically state of equilibrium cannot be achieved within the specified maximum number of iterations, the solution is terminated and labeled non-convergent.

The implemented methods are essentially based on a modified Newton-Raphson technique adopting a constant system stiffness. To assure performance, the procedure is enriched by so-called secant related acceleration strategies (Crisfield / BFGS) which rely on a smart im- provement of the current standard iterative displacement update (stemming from the standard modified Newton-Raphson) according to mathematical methods, that account for information of preceding iteration steps. Doing this, the convergence process is generally accelerated significantly.
 The following procedures are available:
 • Standard Modified Newton-Raphson with initial system stiffness
 • Crisfield Acceleration Method
 • BFGS Acceleration Method
 Control of these methods is achieved via CTRL KITE.
 Default-wise, an additional ’slack’ line-search is applied (cf. subsection 2.5.3).
 The CRISFIELD method is based on a modification of the standard iterative displacement up- date δ∗ of the following form (2-vector-update):
 δ = F · δ∗ + E · δ−1
 (2.16)
 The scaling factor stemming from an optional line-search procedure is, for the sake of clarity, not considered in this notation. Apparently, the new update is composed of the standard up- date and the update from the previous iteration step. The influence of the previous update is accounted for via the factor E. The calculation rules for the factors E and F are not reproduced here – detailed information can be found in Chrisfield [9] and Chrisfield [10]. Setting E = 0 and F = 1 the formulation reduces to the standard update.
 To improve robustness of the solution procedure, permissible ranges for E and F are defined by additional control parameters FMN, FMAX and EMAX, please refer to CTRL KITE.
 While the Crisfield method incorporates additional information −1 from the preceding iteration step only, the BFGS (BROYDEN-FLETCHER-GOLDFARB-SHANNO) method uses information of the preceding k iterations to establish an improved update δ for the current iteration step.

To improve robustness of the solution procedure, permissible ranges for E and F are defined by additional control parameters FMN, FMAX and EMAX, please refer to CTRL KITE.. While the Crisfield method incorporates additional information −1 from the preceding iteration step only, the BFGS (BROYDEN-FLETCHER-GOLDFARB-SHANNO) method uses information of the preceding k iterations to establish an improved update δ for the current iteration step..
 For details of the method, please refer to Crisfield [11] and Luenberger [12].

The line-search procedure aims at modifying the current displacement increment’s step length in such a way that the energy potential is minimized in the current search direction δp . Hence, the essential goal is to find an optimum step length in the current search direction. To this end, a line-search factor η is introduced. The iterative update of the displacements can then be
 = −1 + η · δ.
 (2.17)
 In order to minimize the potential energy we require the scalar product of residual force vec- tor and displacement increment vector (=energy) to vanish, or more practically, to satisfy a specified tolerance. From this condition the line-search factor η can be determined.
 The implementation of the adopted line-search procedure follows the lines given in Crisfield [11].
 The line-search can be very useful to control the solution process for problems that exhibit a volatile nonlinear response.
 Control of the line-search procedure is achieved via CTRL LSRC.

Nonlinear elastoplastic systems are in general sensitive to the magnitude of the load increment (→ formation of plastic zones). For numerical simulations of structures that exhibit a significant nonlinear response, an incremental increase of the system load is reasonable in order to track the nonlinear system response (continuation method). Moreover, such a load stepping ap- proach can also be adopted for limit analyses, e.g., continuous loading of the system until failure occurs, i.e. (numerical) equilibrium can no longer be achieved.
 The backbone of the approach is the introduction of a load level factor λ that scales the effective system load vector Feƒ. Doing this, the system equilibrium condition reads
 The Constant stepping scheme applies a subdivision of the effective system load vector qeƒ into N integral increments of equal magnitude
 Δλ = const. = λm/N .
 (2.19)
 For the adaptive stepping scheme, as a starting point, only the magnitude of the starting in- crement Δλ0 is specified. The magnitude of the subsequent increments Δλn is determined automatically.
 Choice of the increment size is based on the convergence behaviour – a smooth convergence for the current load increment will result in an increase of the increment for the next load step
 Δλn+1 > Δλn
 (2.20)
 Problematic convergence on the other hand will cause the increment to be reduced
 Δλn+1 < Δλn
 (2.21)
 In case convergence is not achieved within the maximum number of iterations, a reduction of the corresponding load increment’s magnitude and a restart of iterations is performed.
 The load stepping procedure is terminated either in case of the maximum load level factor λm being reached, or in case of undershooting the specified minimum step length Δλmn after repeated increment reduction.
 For details regarding step-length control and increment reduction, please refer to Chrisfield [10].

For details regarding step-length control and increment reduction, please refer to Chrisfield [10].. For the adaptive stepping scheme with arc-length control, the residual force iterations for one load step are not carried out at a prescribed constant load level. Instead, the load increment Δλ is considered as an additional variable which is determined by imposing a complementary condition.

 From the provided starting load level factor λ0, the initial arc-length Δ0 is automatically deter- mined. For subsequent steps, Δn+1 is then adapted automatically following the same lines as for the load factor in the standard adaptive scheme, i.e., under account of the convergence behavior of the current loading step n.
 In case convergence is not achieved within the maximum number of iterations, a reduction of the corresponding load increment’s magnitude and a restart of iterations is performed.
 The load stepping procedure is terminated as soon as one of the following criteria is met:

 For further details regarding arc-length control, please refer to Chrisfield [14], May and Duan [13] and Heidkamp [15].

In the context of geotechnical engineering, system failure and/ or system stability is frequently governed by the soil’s shear strength. This notion is reflected by the FELLENIUS rule which defines safety as the ratio between actual shear strength and mobilized shear strength for the system limit state (system state at failure)
 tan | Qj

 ηφ = tn(φmobzed) and ηc = cmobzed (2.23)
 Adopting this concept, the task is to determine the mobilized shear strength – i.e., the shear strength that is actually required to assure balance of a given loading state.
 To this end, the algorithmic framework of the load stepping scheme, initially aiming at a gradual increase of the effective system load, is now used in order to simulate a gradual decrease of the system’s resistance. To illustrate this, Equation 2.18 is rewritten as
 Stepping without arc-length control leaves the adopted safety level ηn constant for each load step n; thus, the procedure incrementally approaches the (most critical) system collapse mech- anism.
 Similar to the load stepping, cf. subsection 2.5.4, the procedure terminates if one of the follow- ing criteria is met:
 • The specified maximum safety level ηm is reached.
 • The specified maximum number of load steps is reached.
 • Undershooting of the specified minimum safety increment Δηmn after repeated load incre- ment reduction.
 After sucessful computation, a sequence of system states is established, each associated with a certain safety level η. Assessing these system states helps to analyze the system’s sensitiv- ity with respect to strength induced failure and also provides some insight into the formation of possible failure mechanisms. Having identified the ultimate permissible system state, the as- sociated safety factor η directly represents the corresponding computational FELLENIUS safety according to Equation 2.23.
 Hint
 It should be noted, that the phi-c reduction technique by no means can replace engineer- ing judgement. It can provide valuable additional information for safety assessment – the assessment itself, however, remains the engineer’s very own task.

The input table defines the structure of a **TALPA** control/data sequence for SOFiSTiK, focused on the **finite element analysis (TASK FEA)** and **construction stage manager geotechnics (TASK CSG)** workflows. It explicitly notes that TALPA can run in **either** mode, but **not both simultaneously**. The record order is arbitrary, implying the parser matches by record “HEAD/END” (described in the general SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual) and then processes the listed records independently.

At the top level the table consists of multiple **records** (e.g., `TASK`, `PHRS`, `PLC`, etc.), each with one or more **items** (keywords/parameters). The first column shows record identifiers; the second column lists the available item keywords accepted for that record.

### Global task/mode selection
- **`TASK` — `OPT`**: selects the operational task/mode. Together with the constraint “CSG and FEA cannot be executed at the same time,” this record governs which geotechnical workflow is active.

### System/control parameters
- **`SYST`** contains fields controlling the problem setup and numerical solution behavior:
  - `TYPE`, `PROB`, `ITER`, `PLC`
  - `OPT`, `VAL`, `FMAX`, `FMIN`, `EMAX`, `EMIN`, `IDES`
  - and options such as `SAVE`, `FACQ`
  These collectively look like solver iteration/limits, scaling factors, and output/save behavior.
- **`CTRL`** is a grouped control record complementing `SYST` (items like `OPT`, `VAL`, `FMAX`, `FMIN`, etc. appear under this record in the table layout), indicating additional parameterization of solution control.
- **`PHRS`**: provides phase-related and load/handling parameters:
  - `HW`, `LC`, `T`
  - `TYPE`, `SIGN`, `GAM A`, `OCR`, `POP` (as shown: `TYPE`, `LC`, `T`, plus sign/strength/dilatancy-like parameters)
- **`PLC` / `TPLC` / `GRP`**: define layered/parameterized “PLC” entities and grouping:
  - `PLC`: `LC`, `TYPE`, `LADD`, `FADD`, `FS2L`
  - `TPLC`: `LC1`, `T1`, `LC2`, `T2`, `TREF`
  - `GRP`: `NO`, `VAL`, `FACS`, `PLC`, `GAM`, `H`, `K`
    plus sign/combination factors: `SIGN`, `SI GH`, `FACL`, `F ACD`, `FACT`, `HW`, `GAMA`, `GFS`, `PLQ`, `FACQ`, `MNO`, `HPLC`, `ALP0`, `HING`, `OCR`, `POP`, `TYPE`, `FACU`, `PTSZ`.
  This suggests `GRP` establishes parameter groups with strength/modification coefficients and reference values tied to the previously defined PLC/phase structure.

### Case/line identifiers and material/geometry factors
- **`LC` record**: appears to define calculation load cases or linear combinations:
  - `NO`, `FACT`, `DLX`, `DLY`, `DLZ`, `T`, `GAMF`
  - additional modifiers: `GAMC`, `CRI3`, `TITL`, `TYPEW`, `GAMF`, `PSI0`, `PSI1`, `PSI2`, `PS1S`, `GAMA`
- **`LCC` record**: another load-case-like aggregator:
  - `NO`, `FACT`, `NOG`, `NFRO`, `NTO`, `NINC`

### History and optional configuration
- **`HIST`**: `TYPE`, `NO` — likely selects a history model/type and an associated identifier.
- **`NSTR`**: `KMOD`, `KSV`, `KSB` — probably selects model/strain/state variables or computation options.
- **`ECHO`**: `OPT`, `VAL` — controls echo/verbosity or logging behavior for the TALPA execution.

### Overall meaning of the structure
In essence, the table documents **which records can appear in the input** and **which parameter keywords each record supports**. The configuration is modular: task selection is handled by `TASK/OPT`, while subsequent records define solver/system controls (`SYST/CTRL`), phase and parameter relationships (`PHRS`, `PLC`, `TPLC`, `GRP`), load case parameters (`LC`, `LCC`), and optional history/logging/model switches (`HIST`, `NSTR`, `ECHO`). The arbitrary record order indicates the input reader relies on record identifiers rather than a strict sequence.

This table is an excerpt of the SOFiSTiK TALPA record/item definition, shown in “Record” / “Items” format. It lists multiple TALPA configuration records (first column) and the allowed or required parameter items for each record (second column). The order of records in the actual input is arbitrary. Two execution modes are referenced in the surrounding context: **Finite Element Analysis (TASK FEA)** and **Construction Stage Manager Geotechnics (TASK CSG)**. Importantly, TALPA processes are configured for **either CSG or FEA, but not both simultaneously**; the records described here are specific to the selected mode(s). Additionally, the meta-records **HEAD** and **END** are handled as described in the general SOFiSTiK manual (“Basics”).

1. **Record: `TASK`**

2. **Record: `CSYS`**

   - Purpose: Defines the coordinate system / problem-related setup for TALPA processing. It likely binds TALPA’s internal operations (e.g., interpretation of subsequent data) to a specific problem definition referenced as `PROB`.

3. **Record: `CCRL`**

- **Role in the overall modeling context:** This temperature anchors how changes in temperature are interpreted in the constitutive updates for concrete and steel during fire loading.

### 3) Keyword: **TCRL**

- **Unit:** Listed as **LIT4** (a selection/control type rather than a physical unit).

  - **C1**: “recovery suppressed”

  - **S0**: “see C0” (i.e., recovery allowed, analogous to concrete’s C0 behavior)

### Contextual meaning for fire behavior
In the accompanying text, default assumptions are consistent with this table:
- **Concrete** generally **does not re-harden or re-stiffen during cooling** (material remains in the most damaged state reached at maximum temperature). This corresponds to the default **C1** (“recovery suppressed”).

The table’s content can be interpreted as a structured set of *configuration rules* and *behavioral options* that govern how material properties evolve during a thermal–mechanical simulation.

## 3.5.9 FIRE Analysis: temperature-dependent behavior and options
This portion describes that the program models temperature evolution of **mechanical strength and stiffness** using a **family of laws** (i.e., *one work law per defined temperature level*). If the user does not explicitly provide temperature-dependent inputs (referenced as “AQUA SSLA”), the program defaults to **EN 1992-1-2:2004**. This implies the table governs whether user overrides exist and which standard laws are used.

Key control concepts and restrictions are stated:
- **User-defined temperature-dependent work laws** can be adopted only when the laws are tied to the **ultimate limit state**. In that case, selection via parameters **NSTR KSV UL(D)** and **KSV KSB UL(D)** inside corresponding **TALPA runs** is mandatory.
- **Warning:** option **EPST SHIFT** is **not allowed** in this context. If enabled, it triggers evaluation based on the *actual temperature level* of each material point.
- Default cooling behavior differs by material:  
  - **Concrete**: assumed **no re-hardening/re-stiffening** on cooling; it remains in the damaged state associated with the **maximum reached temperature**.  
  - **Steel**: assumed to **regain stiffness/strength during cooling**; evaluation uses the **current temperature**.
  - These cooling defaults can be changed via **CTRL FIRE TCRL**.
- **CTRL FIRE** affects only the **fiber beam element**. Temperature profiles may be defined through beam temperature load types (constant/linear across depth), and from a later software update, **general nonlinear profiles** are supported via **BEAM TYPE T EZA**.

Additional modeling assumptions are highlighted:
- Structural fire analysis assumes **concrete carries no tensile stress**. A **temperature-dependent tensile strength reduction** is **not performed** by the program.

## 3.5.10 CONC Concrete material controls
This section is a set of input controls for concrete behavior:
- **Redefinition of material properties** is explicitly **temporary**: it affects only the current analysis run and does **not permanently store** the changes.
- Scope rule: if **no specific material number** is addressed, the redefinition applies to **all concrete materials active in the run**.
- A “Hint” states that choosing **hyperelastic material behavior** may help in fire analysis to model **stress relaxation** caused by stiffness degradation at higher temperatures. It avoids conservation of high constraint stresses from earlier, lower-temperature loading.
- It is clarified that any **permanent temperature-induced degradation** described in the fire analysis section remains unaffected by the hyperelastic choice.

A concrete damage-model interaction is noted:
- For the **fiber beam’s concrete fracture energy-based damage model**, behavior is controlled only by **fracture energy** and **tensile strength**; any provided **tensile branch** in the concrete material law is **ineffective**.

## TSTF: steel–concrete bond behavior (tension stiffening)
The table also includes a control **TSTF** describing automatic steel–concrete bond behavior based on modification of **steel strain** according to cracking state. It defines three phases:
1. **Uncracked state (state I)**
2. **Crack formation phase**
3. **Stabilized cracking (state II)**  
It references secondary literature (CEB) for the procedure and points to an example illustrating the “stiffening” effect due to bond behavior.

Finally, the redefinition rule (temporary, applies to all active concrete materials if no material number is specified) is repeated as a guiding statement.

Overall, the table is best represented in a RAG store as a **configuration/control specification** describing: default vs user-defined temperature law usage, constraints on options, how cooling is treated differently for concrete and steel, how temperature profiles are input, and how concrete and bond-related material behaviors are controlled for fire analyses.

content:
The table describes **material-law algorithm control parameters** for **user-defined nonlinear material models** in SOFiSTiK. In this context, most nonlinear material behavior is formulated in **rate form**: given a **total strain increment**, the program determines the corresponding **stress increment** by **integrating nonlinear strain rates** over the increment. To perform this integration, numerical algorithms are employed—typically **implicit schemes** such as **Backward-Euler**, and in some cases **explicit schemes** such as **Runge-Kutta** or **Forward-Euler**. For **standard materials**, these algorithm control parameters are **internally fixed** and not user-configurable. For **user-defined material models** (referenced as *cf.AQUA: NMAT*), the interface routine **NMAT3D_USD()** allows the user to set **up to five control parameters** via an array **Ctrl**.

The table has columns **MSTE**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. **MSTE** enumerates the parameter names/identifiers, while **Description** maps each identifier to a specific position in the control array:

- **VAL**: **1st parameter → Ctrl(1)**  
  - Default value: **0.0**  
- **FMAX**: **2nd parameter → Ctrl(2)**  
  - Default value: **0.0**  
- **FMIN**: **3rd parameter → Ctrl(3)**  
  - Default value: **0.0**  
- **EMAX**: **4th parameter → Ctrl(4)**  
  - Default value: **0.0**  
- **EMIN**: **5th parameter → Ctrl(5)**  
  - Default value: **0.0**

The **Unit** column lists **“–”** for all entries, indicating that the parameters are treated as **dimensionless control values** (or that units are not specified at this interface level).

Overall, the table’s purpose is to specify **how user-provided algorithm settings are passed** to the nonlinear material integration procedure through **Ctrl(1) to Ctrl(5)**, and it documents that the interface provides **five optional tuning inputs**, all defaulting to **0.0** when the user does not override them.

Most nonlinear material laws (cf.AQUA: NMAT) are formulated in rate form. With a given total strain increment the corresponding stress increment therefore is generally established via in- tegration of the nonlinear strain rates. For this procedure powerful and robust algorithms are used – mostly implicit algorithms (Backward-Euler), in some cases explicit ones (Runge-Kutta, Forward-Euler).
 For the SOFiSTiK standard materials, control parameters of these algorithms are internally preset and not subject to user input.
 For user defined material models (cf.AQUA: NMAT), up to 5 control parameters can be modified by user input. The corresponding input is passed via the interface routine NMAT3D_USD() by means of the array Ctrl.

Prior to storage in the database, the computed displacements of the current load step are scaled by means of the factor provided here. This option is useful in the context of an in-situ stress state computation by means of the K-procedure (gravity loading), which is a common means for geomechanical analyses. In other situations, use of this option is discouraged. The system deformation computed by the K-procedure is of no practical relevance, it is a numerical
 result of generating the desired stress state, only. Specification of CTRL DEFO 0.0 effectively sets the nodal displacements to zero. The option CTRL DEFO ’AUTO’ triggers an automatic decision making procedure. In this case, the nodal displacements are set to zero, if all three subsequent conditions are fulfilled for the respective load step:
 no primary load case is referenced
 the K-procedure is used
 equilibrium (convergence) is achieved

The table defines the parameter **LSEQ** with sub-option **VAL** values that control **load case sequence behavior** in TALPA during operations involving **automatic load or time incrementation** (e.g., `CTRL STEP AUTO...`). In such calculations, intermediate results are saved and also appear as separate load cases with consecutive numbering. However, because the number of increments (and thus the specific load case number of the final increment) is not known in advance, TALPA introduces the concept of **load case sequences** to reliably reference the “final” state as the **primary load case** for subsequent calculation stages (e.g., construction stages). The table notes that control is handled via a **bit scheme**, and to enable both options the input `CTRL LSEQ VAL 3` is used.

### Table structure and columns
- **LSEQ**: The parameter identifier.
- **Description**: Text describing the meaning of each **VAL** bit value.
- **Unit**: Displays a dash (`–`), indicating the parameter is not given in physical units.
- **Default**: The default setting is shown as **0**.

### VAL options (bit-coded)
Under **VAL**, the table lists three key values:

1. **VAL = 0**  
   - Meaning: **No load case sequences active**.  
   - Default behavior: This corresponds to the **default setting** and implies that the special sequence interpretation is disabled.

2. **VAL = +1**  
   - Meaning: A TALPA **primary stress state** specification is interpreted as a **load case sequence**.  
   - Consequence: The system references the **last actual load case** belonging to that sequence.

3. **VAL = +2**  
   - Meaning: The **load case number provided** is instead treated as a **load case sequence number**.  
   - Consequence: The **actual load case number** is chosen automatically based on a possibly preceding, **continuously numbered** load case sequence.

### Combined setting
Because the values are bit-coded, **VAL = 3** enables both **+1** and **+2** behaviors simultaneously. This is explicitly consistent with the surrounding context: using `CTRL LSEQ VAL 3` allows TALPA to (a) treat the primary stress state as a sequence and (b) map a provided identifier to the correct final/actual load case within that sequence, even when increment counts are not predetermined.

For calculations with automatic load or time incrementation (CTRL STEP AUTO...), results of the intermediate steps are normally stored in the data base, as well - as separate load cases with consecutive load case numbers. As a result of the automatic incrementation, the required number of increments is not known a priori - the same holds for the number of the load case representing the final increment. To enable referencing of this load case as primary load case for a subsequent calculation step (construction stage), TALPA uses the concept of load case sequences. Control specification is done according to bit scheme. To enable both options, CTRL LSEQ VAL 3 must be entered.

The table describes the **AFIX** control parameter, which governs how the program handles potentially **undefined or ill-conditioned kinematic degrees of freedom** (DOFs) in a structural/finite-element context. The accompanying context notes that AFIX assigns a priori a **small stiffness** to recognizable undefined DOFs (e.g., **node rotations of a truss**). This prevents the solver from producing **very large displacements** under loads applied to such DOFs.

### Table structure
- **Column 1: AFIX** – lists the possible numeric values (0–7).
- **Column 2: Description** – explains the behavioral consequence for DOFs at each AFIX setting.
- **Column 3: Unit** – shows **“–”**, meaning AFIX is unitless (a discrete control flag).
- **Column 4: Default** – provides the default setting, which is **2**.

### Meaning of AFIX values (0–7)
Each value indicates how the software reacts when it encounters DOFs that are **exactly movable** vs. **movable within numerical precision**, and whether such conditions are treated as **fatal errors** or merely **warnings**. The table can be read as increasing tolerance and/or different handling modes:

- **AFIX = 0**  
  **Exactly movable DOFs** cause an **error message** and **interrupt execution**.
  
- **AFIX = 1** *(Default behavior indicated as separate from default setting)*  
  DOFs movable within the **calculation precision** are **error-announced** and execution is **interrupted**.

- **AFIX = 2** *(Default = 2)*  
  DOFs exactly movable are **suppressed with a warning**, and the program **continues**.

- **AFIX = 3**  
  DOFs movable within calculation precision are **suppressed with a warning**, and execution **continues**.

- **AFIX = 4**  
  Like **0**, but additionally notes that **recognizable undefined DOFs** are provided with a **fixed support**. (So the handling combines strict behavior with stabilization for undefined DOFs.)

- **AFIX = 5**  
  Like **1**, but recognizable undefined DOFs receive a **fixed support**.

- **AFIX = 6**  
  Like **2**, but recognizable undefined DOFs receive a **fixed support**.

- **AFIX = 7**  
  Like **3**, but recognizable undefined DOFs receive a **fixed support**.

### Practical implication
Overall, the table encodes a policy for solver robustness:
- Lower values (0–1) are **strict**: movable DOFs trigger **errors and stop**.
- Mid values (2–3) are more permissive: movable DOFs are **suppressed with warnings**.
- Higher values (4–7) extend the policy for **recognizable undefined DOFs** by **fixing** them (or otherwise constraining them) to avoid unrealistic large displacements, consistent with the provided AFIX context about assigning small stiffness.

AFIX controls the handling of the kinematic degrees of freedom. Recognizable undefined degrees of freedom (e.g. node rotations of a truss) are assigned a priori a small stiffness. Loads corresponding to such degrees of freedom cause very large displacements.

The table defines the **input parameter `CTRL SOLV`** (shown as column **SOLV** with row **VAL**) used in SOFiSTiK to **select the equation solver** for solving finite-element linear systems. It provides four enumerated options, mapping each **numeric value (`VAL`)** to a specific **solver type**. The table also lists the **unit** and **default** settings: the unit is “–” (dimensionless selection code), and the **default value is `3`**.

### Column/row structure
- **Column `SOLV`**: labels the subparameter category as **`VAL`**, meaning the value/code that controls solver selection.
- **Column `Description`**: explains the meaning of each code:
  - `1` corresponds to **Direct Skyline Solver (Gauss/Cholesky)**.
  - `2` corresponds to **Iterative Sparse Solver**.
  - `3` corresponds to **Direct Sparse LDL Solver**.
  - `4` corresponds to **Direct Parallel Sparse Solver (PARDISO)**.
- **Column `Unit`**: uses “–”, indicating no physical unit.
- **Column `Default`**: indicates the default selection is **`3`** (Direct Sparse LDL Solver).

### Solver implications (context)
Although the table itself is only a selection mapping, the surrounding description clarifies key behavioral differences tied to these choices:
- The **Direct Skyline Solver** requires a **skyline-oriented equation numbering** (often achieved via `CTRL OPTI 1` or `CTRL OPTI 2` during system generation) and may need more storage for large 3D problems.
- The **Iterative Sparse Solver** is based on **Conjugate Gradients with preconditioning**; it typically needs less storage but may require more computation depending on convergence behavior and tolerances.
- The **Direct Sparse LDL Solver** is a state-of-the-art direct method (LDL factorization). It typically works efficiently with numbering generated for this solver type to reduce **Fill-In**.
- The **Direct Parallel Sparse Solver (PARDISO)** targets **high performance** using optimized libraries (Intel MKL). It usually offers the least compute time and does not require a priori equation-number optimization, but it has constraints such as limitations in reusing factorized stiffness matrices with other programs.

### Practical meaning of the default
Setting `CTRL SOLV = 3` selects the **Direct Sparse LDL Solver** as the standard choice, reflecting a general preference for robust performance and efficiency in typical finite-element workflows.

The table defines the input parameter set **(CTRL SOLV)** used in SOFiSTiK for solving linear equation systems in the finite-element (Finite-Element) context. It summarizes which **sub-parameters** are available, what each one controls, their **unit** (all are unitless), and the **default values** used by the software.

### Structure of the table
- **Columns:**  
  1) **SOLV**: the parameter name (VAL, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6)  
  2) **Description**: meaning of the parameter and any enumerated options  
  3) **Unit**: given as “–” (no physical unit applies)  
  4) **Default**: default setting used by SOFiSTiK unless the user overrides it

### Parameters and their meaning
- **VAL**: selects the **solver type**. In this table slice, **VAL = 2** corresponds to the **Iterative equation solver** (conjugate gradients, as described in the surrounding text). The default entry is marked “!” indicating that the default for VAL is set/required elsewhere rather than being a simple numeric default in this snippet.

- **V2 (Maximum number of iterations):** controls how many iterations the iterative solver may perform before stopping. Default is “*”, meaning the default exists but is not explicitly stated in the table view.

- **V3 (Tolerance in numeric digits, range 5 to 15):** sets the numerical convergence criterion for the iterative solver. The surrounding context emphasizes that **the solution correctness depends primarily on this tolerance** and therefore **changing the default V3 is not recommended**; analysts should validate results.

- **V4 (Type of preconditioning):** selects the preconditioner used with the conjugate-gradient method. The **default is 1**, i.e., **Incomplete Cholesky**. Options listed are:  
  - **0: Diagonal scaling (not recommended)**  
  - **1: Incomplete Cholesky**  
  - **2: Incomplete Inverse** (noted as generally inferior to Cholesky for convergence and cost, but may perform better for more densely populated matrices; the text suggests a recommendation threshold for V5).

- **V5 (Threshold value of preconditioning):** sets a relative threshold to reduce the number of matrix entries used during preconditioning. Default is “*”. The accompanying narrative connects V5 to performance tuning and notes that the optimal choice is structure-dependent and may require testing.

- **V6 (Maximum bandwidth in preconditioning):** further limits how much of the matrix structure is considered in the preconditioner by restricting maximum bandwidth. Default is “*”. This is another tuning mechanism alongside V5.

### Overall interpretation for RAG
This table is a compact configuration reference for the **iterative solver mode** of **(CTRL SOLV)**, focusing on convergence control (V2, V3), and computational acceleration/stability (V4–V6 through preconditioning). It should be indexed such that queries like “What does V4=1 mean?” or “How does tolerance V3 affect correctness?” retrieve the corresponding row descriptions and the associated defaults/recommendations.

Once the phreatic surface position is known, the program automatically calculates finite element self-weight using either the **specific weight** or the **specific weight under buoyancy**, depending on whether an element lies above or below the phreatic surface (per the AQUA manual, commands **MAT/MATE**).

- **Unit**: `[m]_{1006}`
- **Default**: `-` (no value stated; must be supplied when using the horizontal phreatic level definition)

### Table description: **GRP – Group control and load-step modifiers for element sub-sets**

The table defines **group-wise control parameters** for the record **GRP**. A GRP entry controls which elements participate in the current **calculation/analysis step** (e.g., in simulation of construction stages) and how **stress states and internal forces** are transferred from **primary load cases**. The specification is **valid for all load cases** of the referenced input block.

#### 1) Element group assignment / activation logic
- Each **finite element** is assigned to an **element group** using its **element number**.
- Element grouping can be created with:
  - **equally sized groups** via **group divisor GDIV**, or
  - **variable group sizes**, following the SOFIMSHA concept (see SYST).
- If **no GRP specification** exists, **all elements** are active by default.
- If GRP is specified, then **only the referenced element groups are active**; all other elements are treated as **inactive** for that computation step.
- Within one program run (PROG TALPA), the **default group selection** is inherited from the **previous calculation step**. If group control changes, **element stiffness matrices are reassembled**.

#### 2) Factorization controls (gravity and stiffness)
For the selected group:
- **FACD**: factorizes the group’s **gravity loading** (self-weight), based on the computed self-weight and the specified material densities (GAM/GAMA from AQUA: MAT).
- **FACS**: factorizes the group’s **elastic stiffness** for the current step.

A special relaxation case (often in tunneling) is described:
- **FACL = FACS = FACG (= FACU) = α**, with **0 < α < 1**, enabling a common calibration/relaxation factor.

#### 3) Primary state references (PLC / FACL / stress adoption)
- **PLC** references the **construction stage / primary load case number** that the current step is based on. It defaults to the global **PLC**.
- If an element group is **not meant** to reference a regular primary state, **PLC 0** or **PLC 'SITU'** must be used.
- **PLC 'SITU'** is motivated by the Hardening Plasticity Soil Model:
  - hardening behavior is **deactivated** for the referenced elements for that load step,
  - strength properties remain unaffected,
  - after equilibrium, the model performs **automatic calibration of internal hardening parameters** to match the achieved stress state.
- **FACL** controls whether and how **internal forces and stress state** are adopted from the referenced primary load case (concept of “primary states” referenced in section 2.4.1).

#### 4) In-situ stress initialization and groundwater level
- The table supports defining initial stresses either via:
  - **K-procedure** (requires only lateral earth pressure coefficient **K**; GAM/GAMA, H, SIGN and SIGH not applicable), or
  - **analytical primary stress state**, requiring **K**, **GAM/GAMA**, **H**, **SIGN**, and optionally **SIGH**.
- **Important admissibility rule**: providing in-situ stress parameters (K, GAM, GAMA, H, SIGN, SIGH) is inadmissible if the group already references a regular primary stress state (GRP … PLF).
- **HW** specifies **groundwater level per group**:
  - elements whose center points lie **below HW** receive **buoyancy forces**,
  - implemented using the buoyant specific weight via **GAMA**.
  - default: **HW = infinite depth**.
- Analytical primary stress calculation uses **GAMA from the GRP input**.

#### 5) Two-phase model activation and pore pressure initialization
The table also contains controls that activate the **2-phase approach** for continuum elements (QUAD under plane strain or axial symmetry):
- **TYPE** options:
  - **UNDR** (undrained): pore water flow suppressed → pore water contributes to bulk stiffness; volumetric deformation may create/change excess pore pressures.
  - **DRAI** (drained): flow unrestrained → no pore water stiffness contribution; excess pore pressures vanish (FACU = 0).
  - **NONP**: non-porous; material behavior independent of pore water content.
- For 2-phase behavior to be active:
  - corresponding **undrained material properties** (from AQUA: NMAT.UNDR) must exist, and
  - **TYPE UNDR/DRAI** must be specified; otherwise the element is treated as non-porous.
- **FACU** initializes **excess pore water pressures** for the present step by factorizing those from the referenced primary load case:
  - defaults depend on TYPE:
    - **FACU = 1.0** for **TYPE UNDR**
    - **FACU = 0.0** for **TYPE DRAI**
  
#### 6) Temperature load, hydratation, swelling, hinge deactivation
Additional group-wise modifiers:
- **TPLC**: imports a temperature field from HYDRA to compute stresses for temperature loading; requires **FACT = 1.0** for activation.
- Hydration-dependent stiffness:
  - represented via a reference to the hydration load case (HYDRA),
  - through **HPLC lc ALP0 alpha0**, where **alpha0** is the lower threshold for stiffness development.
- **Swelling activation**:
  - **PLQ** defines the primary load case for swelling (state is equilibrium using swelling material model NMAT SWEL),
  - **FACQ** scales swelling effect; default is **0.0** (swelling inactive unless FACQ ≠ 0).
- **HING**: element-group-wise deactivation of beam hinge effects during system generation, affecting both explicit and implicit hinges.

Overall, this table provides a **comprehensive mechanism** to: (a) select element subsets for a stage, (b) scale gravity and stiffness, (c) map stress/internal forces from primary states (including special in-situ and hardening-calibration logic), and (d) optionally activate coupled effects (groundwater pore pressures, temperature/hydration, swelling, hinge suppression).

This table defines the fields of an input record used to **activate a load case** and control how subsequent load definitions are interpreted and scaled during analysis. The record introduces a set of **global modifiers** (factors, time stepping, soil/material safety factors, and load combination coefficients) that apply to all loads assigned to the active load case.

#### Core load case control
- **NO (Load case number)**: Identifier of the load case. Default is **1**. This field selects which load case subsequent loads belong to.
- **FACT (Factor for all loads)**: Global multiplicative factor applied to loads in the active load case. Default is **1.0**.  
  **Important exception behavior:** FACT “in principle affects all loads,” but it **does not apply** to:
  - temperature loading,
  - strain loading,
  - prestressing loads,
  - gravity loading components (**DLX, DLY**).  
  Dead load in the X/Y directions can therefore be governed independently (see DLX/DLY).

#### Dead load direction scaling
- **DLX (Dead load factor in global X direction)**: Default **0.0**.
- **DLY (Dead load factor in global Y direction)**: Default **0.0**.
- **DLZ (Dead load factor in global Z direction)**: Default **0.0**.  
These factors represent how much dead load is applied in each global axis direction for the load case, and they are explicitly treated separately from FACT.

Additionally, the context indicates dead load may also be specified via a **group control record (GRP)**. If a groundwater level is provided in GRP, the program distinguishes:
- regular dead load and
- dead load under buoyancy.

**Compatibility note:** **DLZ** exists for compatibility with programs **SEPP** and **ASE** and **cannot be used with TALPA**.

#### Time stepping and incremental interpretation
- **DT (Time period of total load step [sec])**: Default **0.0**.  
  The value represents the **total increment** for the load step and may be further subdivided in an **incremental calculation** controlled by a separate setting (CTRL STEP). It is especially relevant for **time-dependent material laws**.
  
Context also references **VAL** (interpreted as the time period Δt for the load step) and states it may be interpreted as a total increment.

#### Soil/material safety factors (general material laws)
- **GFRI (Safety factor for friction)**: Default **1.0**.
- **GCOH (Safety factor for strength/cohesion)**: Default **1.0**.  
These are relevant for **all general soil/material laws**. In incremental calculations, they are **linearly interpolated** between:
- the initial state, and
- the provided value.

#### Post-processing criterion
- **CRIA3 (Free criteria for post processing)**: Default **0.0**.  
A numeric parameter used to tag or control post-processing evaluation criteria.

#### Title and action/combinations linkage
- **TITL (Title of load case)**: Default **LIT24** (asterisk indicates it may be autogenerated depending on settings).  
  If no TITL is given, the program may **automatically generate a title** from the sum of activated forces and/or increment details (especially for incremental calculations).

- **TYPE (Designation of the action)**: No default listed; default shown as “-”.  
  This field can predefine the **action type** and associated **safety factors/combination coefficients** for later **superposition with MAXIMA**. Several literals for TYPE are defined in the ACT record of SOFiLOAD; this table allows alternative parameters to be supplied here as needed.

#### Combination parameters for superposition / design scenarios
These fields define safety/combination factors used for various load combinations. Defaults are indicated as “*”, meaning they are typically dependent on other defaults or program logic:

- **GAME (Favourable safety factor)**
- **PS0 (Rare combination value rare)**
- **PS1 (Frequent combination value frequent)**
- **PS2 (Quasi-permanent combination value)**

Context clarifies that if superposition factors are defined via **SOFiLOAD or MAXIMA**, then parameters **TYPE to PS1S** should **not** be specified here.

#### Accidental load factor
- **GAMA (Safety factor accidental)**: Default “*”.  
Used for accidental design situations (part of the combination/safety framework).

The table defines a set of input parameters used when creating or modifying a load case, with emphasis on selecting and copying subsets of loads between load cases. It contains four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. The “Item” column lists the parameter names as abbreviations, while the “Description” column explains their role. The “Unit” column is shown as “–” for all parameters, indicating these inputs are not physical quantities. The “Default” column specifies either a numeric default or a dependency-based default.

**Row-by-row meaning:**
- **NO**: “Number of an already defined load case.” This parameter references the source load case used for operations such as copying (context: LC/LCC described in the accompanying text). The default is marked with **“!”**, indicating that **NO is mandatory** and must be provided by the user.
- **FAKT**: “Load factor.” This factor scales the loads being transferred/copied into the current load case. The default is **1.0**, meaning loads are copied without scaling unless overridden. The context further clarifies that when a load factor is applied, loads are stored in the database as **resultants**, and therefore any originally specified load factor cannot be distinguished after storage.
- **NOG**: “Group number for loaded elements.” This supports selection of element loads **group-wise** (as described in the context: for element loads, **NOG can be used** to select a group). The default is **“–”**, meaning no value is selected by default, and its use depends on the selection needs.
- **NFRO**: “Smallest node number.” This defines the start of a node range used for selecting **nodal loads** when copying. The default is **“–”**, implying it must be relevant to the intended region selection.
- **NTO**: “Largest node number.” This defines the end of the node range used for the same nodal-load selection. Its default is given as **NFRO**, meaning if not explicitly set, the range may collapse to a single node or rely on NFRO.
- **NINC**: “Increment of node numbers.” This controls stepping through nodes in the range (e.g., selecting every NINC-th node). The default is **1**, meaning all nodes in the specified range are considered.

**Selection logic (from the referenced context):**
- For **nodal loads**, only specific loads are copied by selecting a node region from **NFRO to NTO**, using **NINC** as the step size.
- For **element loads**, selection can be performed via **NOG** for element group-wise selection.
- Load copying includes all loads except gravity loads **DLX–DLZ**, and the copied loads may be multiplied by **FAKT** during the operation.

Overall, the table serves as a compact definition of the parameter set controlling *which loads* (by load case reference and region/group selection) are copied and *how strongly* they are scaled when transferred.
